$comment: KJC-TSK-0703: the canonical prompt-injection catalog of the karajan family. Data, not code: each language keeps only its small scanning engine. Expressions must stay portable (JavaScript RegExp and Python re): invisible characters go as literal characters (JSON escapes), never as regex escapes like \u{...}; flags are only i, m, s, u. Bump version on any change.

patterns.why: Tells the model to drop the instructions it was given, the classic override.
Same override as ignore-previous, worded to slip past a single keyword.
Asks the model to wipe its context or rules before obeying new ones.
Names the system or reviewer prompt as something to replace.
Negates the instructions above it, steering the model away from its task.
Announces a fresh instruction block inside content that should carry none.
Forges a system message that redefines who the model is.
Role reassignment: asks the model to become another persona.
Role reassignment phrased as a fact the model should accept.
Installs a standing behaviour change for the rest of the conversation.
Role-play framing used to step around the model's instructions.
Dictates the reviewer's verdict instead of letting it judge the change.
Fixes the output to approved whatever the content says.
Tries to write the verdict field directly.
A forged approved verdict next to an instruction to ignore something.
Hands the model a ready answer to emit instead of its own.
Same as output-json: a scripted response smuggled into the content.
Zero-width spaces and LTR/RTL marks hide text a human reviewer cannot see.
Bidi embedding and override characters reorder what is displayed (Trojan Source).
Bidi isolates, the other half of the Trojan Source trick.
A byte order mark in the middle of text is invisible and has no honest use there.
Runs of soft hyphens split words so keyword filters miss them.
Word joiner and invisible operators carry no visible glyph.
Unicode tag characters (U+E0000 to U+E007F) can encode a whole hidden instruction.
An oversized C-style comment can hide a payload addressed to the model.
An oversized HTML comment is invisible when rendered but read by the model.
An oversized Python docstring can carry instructions as prose.
Same as the double-quoted docstring, with single quotes.
An oversized Ruby block comment, the same hiding place.
